It’s been a wild ride for Google Pixel’s App Lock feature, but the tech giant is officially re-releasing the feature today, right alongside its debut on Samsung Galaxy devices.

App Lock debuted on Google Pixel in an August build of Android 17 QPR2’s beta. The feature lets users hide apps behind a biometric or PIN authentication layer while also hiding notifications, widgets, and data from AI services. It’s a useful privacy features, but one that Google removed in subsequent updates. The feature later returned in QPR3 Beta 3 last month, and today Google is officially re-releasing it.

The feature is still only in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 3 for Google Pixel devices, an update that should be released to the stable track in early 2027.

Pixel owners on stable Android 17 QPR2 should already have this! Why would Google make Pixel owners wait until March 2027 to get this?! Release it now to Pixel owners. 🤨.

You can still access App Lock by long-pressing on an app icon and adding it to the app lock list.

In a post on Reddit, Google’s Community Engagement Manager details that App Lock on Google Pixel was removed for improvements before getting a full release:.

…the product team decided to temporarily pull back the feature from the QPR2 Beta to allow for additional polish, thorough testing, and robust integration across all system surfaces.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why Samsung’s One UI 9.5 beta release today also brings support for App Lock. The feature is built into Android 17 QPR2, seemingly the release that One UI 9.5 is based on, but Google Pixel devices aren’t getting it until QPR3. As far as release timelines go, this means that Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series will probably ship with this feature out of the box, where Pixel phones won’t get it until around March or so. One UI 9.5 won’t roll out for older Galaxy devices until May, if One UI 8.5 serves as an example.

It has been revealed that sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

This tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

Sources indicate that the 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint states so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

Sources indicate that the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Industry observers note that here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

In a recent development, the defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

Sources indicate that setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Industry observers note that store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF shows what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

It has been revealed that A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Recent findings suggest that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Sources indicate that across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

The send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola has kicked off its Android 17 rollout for the Razr Fold, marking the first major update for the tech giant’s first book-style foldable, and the start of a potentially interest 7 years of software support.

The Motorola Razr Fold rolled out with Android 16 back in May 2026, and it remains a really good option for those looking to pick up a book-style foldable in the US. On top of solid specs across the board, it also carries the promise of 7 years of software support, something that few other Moto devices can tout.

According to recent reports, but nowhere was it promises that Motorola would speed things up at all. A little over 3 months after Motorola announced the enhancement and several weeks after other Motorola devices were updated to Android 17, the Motorola Razr Fold is finally getting its own Android 17 update.

Recent findings suggest that rolling out now, Android 17 for the Razr Fold is a 4.15GB~ update that appears to be available at least somewhat broadly. Reports are popping up on Reddit including one report from the EU (Hungary, specifically), with another user apparently in a Spanish-speaking region also seeing the update.

Recent findings suggest that we’re still waiting to see if the update is available in the US (there’s a backlog of updates on our unit), but it’s certainly an update to look forward to. Apparently, Motorola finally fixed a weird UI issue that affected the Telegram app, something we ran into when using the device earlier this year.

According to recent reports, it’s great to see the patch out, but it’s noteworthy that Motorola is not setting a particularly encouraging precedent here. Razr Fold is one of the tech giant’s first devices to be promised 7 years of OS updates and software support, and its flagship-tier status certainly would have most expecting it to be updated ahead of some of Motorola’s more affordable, lower-tier devices that were updated over a month ago. Whatever the case, hopefully Motorola will speed things up over the next few years, especially with its $1,600 flagship Signature 27 on the horizon with the same software promises.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A streamer’s PS5 began smoking while they were away for a toilet break mid-way through their play through of GTA 6.

GTA 6 finally debuted on November 19, following years of anticipation, with millions of players diving into Rockstar’s latest open-world blockbuster.

Sources indicate that however, the launch hasn’t been entirely smooth, with PS5 and Xbox players reporting game-breaking crashes. Some have encountered recurring errors that prevent them from progressing, while others have been unable to get past the opening minutes of the game.

On November 21, Twitch streamer JoJoJosiah took to X to share news that their PS5 had begun smoking during a GTA 6 livestream, apparently leaving the console unusable.

Sources indicate that “Was playing GTA VI on stream but had to go poop,” they explained. “Paused it and put on a sensory vid for my chat.”.

However, while they were away, the streamer claimed their “PS5 started just smoking out its a**.” The post was accompanied by a video of the incident.

In the video, JoJoJosiah arrives back at their streaming setup to find the room filled with smoke, while they panic and figure out what to do, before the fire alarm goes off.

Sources indicate that was playing gta VI on stream but had to go poop. Paused it and put on a sensory vid for my chatPS5 started just smoking out its ass and now i need to get a replacement 😀 pic.twitter.com/qSdfcCi4l1.

In a reply to the original tweet, the streamer stated that they were uninjured as a result of the fire. “I’m fine and everything is good tho,” they wrote.

It’s still unclear what caused the console to malfunction, or whether GTA 6 itself played any role in the reported hardware failure, but the streamer revealed that they now need to purchase a replacement console as a result.

Thousands of vulnerable fridges patched against cyberattacks in secret operation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, following devastating hacks that caused European fridges to reach 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks, the UK has implemented nationwide patching to ensure similar attacks won't affect its fridges.
  • Refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions were the first to identify the glitch before the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) all became involved in working on the problem.
  • It has been revealed that "From a business perspective, it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, following devastating hacks that caused European fridges to reach 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks, the UK has implemented nationwide patching to ensure similar attacks won't affect its fridges. While it was thought that the UK had avoided similar hacks because it used different devices from those used in mainland Europe, an even worse glitch was just waiting to be discovered. The BBC reports that a different flaw was discovered by security researchers in late October, one that could have caused even worse damage if it had been identified by hackers. Since then, work has been carried out to harden security across the U.K., with fridges in supermarkets, warehouses, and elsewhere now protected.

Refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions were the first to identify the glitch before the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) all became involved in working on the problem. As a precaution, thousands of devices that control tens of thousands of fridges were blocked from accessing the internet, with supermarket IT workers scrambling to sometimes physically isolate devices by removing network cables.

It has been revealed that "From a business perspective, it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," one supermarket worker warned.

Recent findings suggest that the problem that they were trying to address rested within the most popular refrigeration controllers used across the U.K., made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM). It was found that these controllers had a similar authentication security flaw to those hacked across Europe, although RDM points out that hacking its devices would have required a specific piece of hardware. However, that hardware is freely available.

RDM has since confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on any of its controllers throughout the patching process.

According to recent reports, the situation in France, Belgium, and other European countries was much more dire. After initially hitting France in October, a further wave of attacks swept through supermarkets and even blood banks. Even the fridges at a U.S. military base were not safe. While no responsibility for the attacks has been taken, France has so far laid the blame at the door of Iran — something the country's government denies.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

Industry observers note that the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

It has been revealed that typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

It has been revealed that the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly key when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

In a recent development, zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two vital parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

For a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/owners.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a latest optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

Recent findings suggest that these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a company might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

This becomes particularly crucial when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every vital API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

According to recent reports, API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

You do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document notable endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

A Louisiana coffee shop co-owner claims she refused to serve a TikTok creator who returned to her Baton Rouge cafe after posting two negative reviews.

According to recent reports, victoria Arroyo co-owns Pura Vida Coffee Bar, a cafe near Louisiana State University. TikTok creator Fabian Beaucoudray had criticized the shop’s coffee and food in earlier videos, and Arroyo included clips from those reviews in her response.

In one review she also posted to Snapchat, Beaucoudray noted she went back to give the cafe a second chance. She took glitch with paying $3 for what she described as five small pieces of potato alongside a $10 sandwich.

Sources indicate that beaucoudray posted about being refused service on November 19. She had returned to the cafe with a friend, according to a recap from TikTok creator thenameisblossom. Beaucoudray wrote in the caption of her own video that she had “never seen a company take a bad review this serious.”.

It has been revealed that arroyo said she was working the register when she recognized Beaucoudray and decided to turn her away. According to Arroyo, Beaucoudray had left both times without mentioning her complaints to staff. Arroyo said that she left the shop without a chance to address the problems before the videos went up.

Sources indicate that arroyo tagged Beaucoudray in her November 20 response and addressed her directly in the caption. “I am genuinely sorry if you were embarrassed today, that was never my intention,” she wrote.

Arroyo’s response passed one million views, while some commenters defended her decision, and others said the videos made them want to visit the shop.

Sources indicate that another TikTok food reviewer drew a public response after criticizing the coffee at a Phoenix bakery. In Atlanta, Keith Lee went viral after his family was refused service at The Real Milk and Honey.

Tech Report: Phison details SSD with a built-in NPU and 64GB of memory that supports AI frameworks on the drive

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that phison detailed two new enterprise SSD designs at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26) that aim to answer two separate problems: one with a built-in NPU and 64GB of 130 GB/s memory that supports running PyTorch, vLLM, OpenVINO, and llama.cpp directly on the drive, and another that merges fast pSLC cache with large QLC capacity behind just one controller.
  • In a recent development, the computational-storage design’s premise is that a server can offload more to the SSD, which runs AI code on the data where it already resides and sends back results, instead of whole datasets.
  • In a recent development, phison says that the integrated NPU is expected to deliver “36,800 DMIPS of compute performance,” or Dhrystone Million Instructions Per Second, a typical synthetic benchmark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that phison detailed two new enterprise SSD designs at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26) that aim to answer two separate problems: one with a built-in NPU and 64GB of 130 GB/s memory that supports running PyTorch, vLLM, OpenVINO, and llama.cpp directly on the drive, and another that merges fast pSLC cache with large QLC capacity behind just one controller. The company notes that “many of the products and features mentioned are still in development” and will arrive once finalized.

In a recent development, the computational-storage design’s premise is that a server can offload more to the SSD, which runs AI code on the data where it already resides and sends back results, instead of whole datasets. The pSLC-QLC design, meanwhile, puts the cache inside each drive, which may reduce system complexity, as every drive bay contributes usable capacity and none goes to dedicated cache drives.

In a recent development, phison says that the integrated NPU is expected to deliver “36,800 DMIPS of compute performance,” or Dhrystone Million Instructions Per Second, a typical synthetic benchmark. This is admittedly an old CPU integer benchmark from the 1980s, while NPUs tend to be rated in TOPS, but that figure was not given. For reference, the Topaz NPU add-in card Phison demonstrated at Computex carried eight NPUs rated at up to 40 TOPS each. The DMIPS figure therefore likely refers to, instead, the CPU cores that work alongside it, which we would expect to be based on an Arm Cortex design, adequate for running an SSD of this class but no measure of its AI capability.

The memory and its bandwidth are more crucial for the expected workload, anyway, and while the organization doesn’t state the type, LPDDR5X is a popular option and may be used with the Topaz NPU, according to one secondary report. If the drive is a PCIe 6.0 part comparable to Phison’s X3 controller, it could hit up to 28 GB/s to the host, which would put the memory above 4x that speed. For reference, 130 GB/s is a bit less than half of that of the DGX Spark’s hardware, designed for AI development.

Phison says developers can build on the drive “without specialized programming tools,” which, in this case, is a good thing. The drive does, of course, support multiple general-purpose inference servers and runtimes, but nothing was disclosed about how a host reaches the drive’s compute. The drives “scan and process data in parallel,” which indicates scalability, and return “relevant results” which Phison claims could mean 10 to 100 times less data transferred for applicable workloads. This may free up the host CPU for other tasks.

Recent findings suggest that phison’s idea to put compute on storage isn’t upcoming. Samsung tried this with its SmartSSD — where an FPGA sat on the drive to process data without moving it — which was shown in 2018. Later, in 2022, the design was refined with AMD’s Xilinx Versal FPGA in its second generation, with Samsung claiming more than 50% lower processing time, up to 70% lower energy consumption, and up to 97% lower server CPU usage for scan-heavy database queries, compared to conventional SSDs. The drive has reportedly since disappeared from Samsung’s lineup, though the first-generation model was still sold under AMD’s Xilinx name as of last year.

Recent findings suggest that scaleFlux took a narrower route, with compression handled inside the SSD controller. The server doesn’t see this, so the drive looks like any other NVMe SSD, and no application has to change its behavior. The CEO claims it is the only manufacturer with computational storage in production at hyperscalers. This suggests that not making customers write latest code for the drive is the secret to success, as SmartSSD needed that for its FPGA and for each workload. Phison’s selling point here is flexibility for the client to use code written for common AI frameworks.

Tech giant CTO Sebastien Jean, writing in All About Circuits in 2025, argued that generic computational storage had stalled because “each use case is highly unique and it’s simply not scalable.” He called the idea of running the Linux operating system on a drive with bigger processors a “pie-in-the-sky approach.”.

Accelerators have long been widely used in data centers, and Jean’s proposal was to put targeted ones inside the SSD, each running a set operation over a range of logical block addresses (LBAs). By his reckoning, a chassis with 90 PCIe 6.0 SSDs could process data at 2.5 TB/s without affecting the CPU. The design revealed at SC26, though, appears closer to the general-purpose model, possibly due to the increasing relevance of AI and the demand for both memory and compute.

Jean also spoke at the Emerging Storage Technology panel at the conference to discuss future developments, including PCIe 7.0 drives that would operate at “50, 56 gigabytes per second,” which he called “faster than a DDR channel.” With 32 drives at this speed, a single chassis could reach “1.8 terabytes per second.” He described this specifically as computational storage for HPC.

Turning to the Mixed Media solution, that’s the “high-endurance pSLC and high-capacity QLC flash” SSD; it’s a 16-channel part, so not comparable to anything you see in retail. The pSLC portion of the drive has the 4-bit QLC flash act in a 1-bit SLC mode, which trades space for performance and endurance. Phison says the design builds on standard NVMe interfaces and fits into existing infrastructure “without requiring specialized host software.”.

It has been revealed that jean elaborated at the same panel that the “endurance group on the drive, which is SLC,” is managed separately from the XLC — 3-bit TLC or 4-bit QLC — and each region gets a namespace, so it appears as multiple drives to the OS. Then, high-write data can be sent specifically to the SLC group, while data in the QLC is likely to be more read-heavy. This follows a general trend of enterprise shifting toward QLC for capacity, but having some of it in SLC mode can help reduce the need for specialized caching.

Right now, high-capacity SSDs usually have separate SSDs to fulfill this role, but that takes up more drive bays. The tradeoff with Phison’s approach is that a single drive failure takes out both capacity and a share of the cache. That noted, Phison’s approach is more robust from a cache perspective, as “losing one drive out of 24 would result in a 4% cache loss instead of a 25% loss,” the manufacturer indicates, with the 25% presumably assuming four dedicated cache drives.

Dedicated cache drives need tiering handled by the host or array software, while with Mixed Media each drive holds both tiers and the host simply picks the namespace it wants to write to.

The company is not the first to have this idea, either, as Kioxia presented its Mixed Mode idea during FMS 2025, where each drive has a ratio of pSLC to QLC, set once per drive when it’s first used. Kioxia called 1:4 a “good beginning ratio,” though it mentioned customers typically want pSLC at just 0.5% to 2% of maximum QLC capacity. That implementation also had parity protection on the pSLC space across multiple drives. Kioxia similarly marketed the benefit of needing fewer slots and field-replaceable units (FRUs), and its slides even used the term “Mixed Media” in two chart headings.

DapuStor went further with its dual-mode J5060, a QLC SSD with a pSLC region that was in customer validation as of August; it compared the design against “four dedicated SLC drives” in a 24-drive system, the kind of setup that would produce Phison’s 25% figure. Solidigm’s Cloud Storage Acceleration Layer works differently, with a host-side flash translation layer, where it can manage small writes on SLC or TLC drives before writing to QLC in favorable large sequential chunks.

There’s also the Enmotus FuzeDrive P200, previewed at CES 2020 as the MiDrive, which used a Phison controller and seems to be the closest to an ancestor of the current Mixed Media. That consumer drive, which we reviewed in 2021, had SLC and QLC portions that acted distinctly, but they were managed by Enmotus software.

In every drive, behind one 16-channel controller.

Separate NVMe endurance groups assigned to namespaces; no specialized host software, Phison states.

In every drive, with parity protection on the pSLC space across drives.

1:4 as a “good beginning ratio”; customers typically want pSLC at 0.5% to 2% of maximum QLC capacity.

Ratio set once, creating a pSLC namespace and endurance group.

In every drive, as a pSLC region beside the QLC.

400GB, 800GB or 1.2TB of pSLC on a 30.72TB drive.

Separate SLC and QLC block devices on one drive.

In the drive, as a fixed SLC portion of a consumer QLC SSD.

On dedicated SLC or TLC cache drives.

Reference system: three 800GB SLC drives and seven 61.44TB QLC drives.

Flash translation layer running on the host.

Sources indicate that it’s also inevitable that these two approaches will be compared to Phison’s other upcoming part, the X3 enterprise SSD controller, a PCIe 6.0 design promising up to 28 GB/s of sequential throughput and 6.8 million IOPS. Those figures are unchanged since Computex in June.

According to recent reports, the X3’s IOPS sounds like a lot, but we’ve heard considerable banter about AI needing way more than that, as Nvidia’s roadmap target for PCIe 7.0 is at 100 million IOPS, though that target counts 512-byte reads, a smaller unit than the 4KB that SSD ratings usually use, so the two figures aren’t directly comparable. Jean said at the panel that Phison is “very optimistic” it can achieve that. He added that the eightfold jump in IOPS that comes with moving from 4KB to 512-byte accesses would, on existing NAND, mean “eight times as much power,” or “roughly in the 140 to 180 watt range,” which is beyond reasonable, so perhaps a different solution will be required.

According to recent reports, for the X3, Phison told us in June to expect customer samples by the end of the year, with volume coming in the middle of next year, though the SC26 release gives no dates. Notably, Micron and Samsung are already offering PCIe 6.0 SSDs, and the Bravera SC6 controller is expected from Marvell. Phison also says its PS7161, which its site lists as a customer sample, is “the first PCIe 6.0 redriver on the PCI-SIG Integrators List.”.

Of the two designs, Mixed Media looks like the nearer product. It builds on standard NVMe features, and DapuStor’s similar dual-mode drive reached customer testing this summer, while the one processor figure given for the computational-storage drive notes little about what it can do for AI. What remains to be seen for Mixed Media is its pSLC-to-QLC ratio and how configurable it is. CES and Computex are the notable dates on the 2027 calendar to find out more about both, as well as the X3.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous concerns here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

Industry observers note that not sure if you’ve heard, but the biggest video game of all time is out today: buying Anthropic stock. Yes, in case you haven’t already blown all of your money on the GTA VI Ultimate Edition, you can try your luck at buying one of the most anticipated IPOs of all time when ANT goes public on the Nasdaq later today.

In a recent development, but you’re likely up, playing the game that is, according to Metacritic, already among the best of all time. It’s presently sitting at a near-perfect 99/100 on the aggregator, with reviewers calling it “a masterpiece” and “gaming’s… greatest love story.” It’s a game in which you can do basically anything you want, from the violent to the vacuous.

More than anything, though, I’m just excited to discover all the different ways the game allows you to find and consume coffee.

As I’m sure happened in every newsroom, the conversation this week turned to whether traffic will meaningfully decline today as up to 1.5 million people “call in sick” to play GTA VI. If you’ve been awake since the crack of dawn trying to meander your way to Vice City, you’re just one of many folks experiencing the rarest of moments in 2026: a singular, unifying cultural event.

My biggest question isn’t whether gamers will play GTA VI but whether normies will. Previous games in the series, particularly GTA V, sold hundreds of millions of copies and still draw countless players today. GTA VI feels even more inviting to those who just want to spend time in its sandbox to do some fishing, dancing, or flying. One reviewer even called it a “cozy game” where he just spent time walking around a zoo.

While the size, scale, and impact of GTA VI are exponentially higher, the last time I heard people talking about a game in this way was during the pandemic, when everyone was hunkering down for a winter of Animal Crossing.

Industry observers note that by the way, GTA VI has a functioning smartphone that can be used for making calls, sending texts, taking photos, looking at “Instagram,” and setting reminders, among other things. It’s yet another minor detail in a game full of them. Plus, it looks like an original Pixel.

According to recent reports, usually with sponsored content, I have to spend the whole time convincing you that the product is worth buying. But RedPocket’s Black Friday deals do all that work on their own.

Not only do you get amazing discounts for the first 12 months of service by prepaying for a full year, but RedPocket’s “Lock-in Low” promise means that you get to stay as close to that promotional price as possible once the first year is over.

There’s no contract and no port-in requirement. You can keep your number, keep your phone, and activate with an eSIM on compatible devices. During the Black Friday sale, there’s even a Refer-a-Friend credit that gets you $25 for every person you bring to the service.

According to recent reports, explore RedPocket’s plans or compare the annual offers. This is one of the best Black Friday decisions you’re going to make this month, and maybe ever.

In a recent development, google has finally rolled out its answer to Grok Bot, ChatGPT Dots, and Claude Duet, and it’s called… Tasks? Spark has transitioned to Tasks, and the features are rolling out in six countries for all free Gemini users. I’ll have more to say about this next week.

It has been revealed that also interesting is that Google has released yet another AI model, called Neon, that essentially fits between its brand latest Carbon model (which isn’t yet widely available, and which ostensibly replaces Argon) and Hydrogen. Confused yet? Don’t be. It’s easy.

If older (and freer) games are more to your taste, someone ported Unreal Tournament 2004 to the browser, where I just spent a few minutes reliving some of my favorite gaming moments of my youth.

These charts showing Nvidia’s growth over the past few years are astounding, enraging, and a little scary. Those are big numbers.

On this week’s Sideload, we hosted Eric Migicovsky of Pebble fame to ask him about his newest products, the Pebble Time 2 and Pebble Round 2, along with his feelings on AI and the current state of the tech industry.

Finally, at this year’s DealBook Summit, Andrew Ross Sorkin interviewed a cavalcade of famous people, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Zohran Mamdani, David Ellison, and Mark Carney.

The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

In a recent development, TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real owners can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

According to recent reports, lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

According to recent reports, base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every plan, Free included.

Recent findings suggest that base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

Bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

It has been revealed that replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

Recent findings suggest that v0's Free strategy gives new people $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Sources indicate that figma's Starter blueprint is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

According to recent reports, collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Sources indicate that softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

In a recent development, three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Sources indicate that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human owners.

Building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

Industry observers note that the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of elderly residents at a retirement home in France have been introduced GTA 6, and some are already hoping to get their hands on the game for Christmas.

Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6 finally launched on November 19, 2026, more than 13 years after the release of GTA 5.

Sources indicate that the open-world crime game has attracted enormous attention worldwide, with fans taking time off work to play it. According to French broadcaster TF1, requests for annual leave in France increased by 8% around the game’s launch. Now, the game has been introduced to the older generations.

On November 20, residents at the Domitys senior living facility in Serris, Seine-et-Marne, were introduced to GTA 6 as part of an organized gaming session.

As reported by ICI Paris Île-de-France, the residents swapped their usual activities for an opportunity to explore the game’s virtual world, with many particularly enjoying its boat-driving sequences.

In a recent development, 82-year-old Jacqueline was among the most enthusiastic participants, successfully collecting two packages of cocaine during a mission. “I had never touched a controller before 9am this morning. And by 2:30pm, I was fishing out two packages of drugs,” she joked.

Another resident, 86-year-old Lucienne, was equally impressed by the game’s visuals, describing them as incredible and comparing the experience to watching a real film.

Meanwhile, 75-year-old Yvan admitted that the controls were difficult to master, joking that he was no longer 20 and struggled to keep up with the action.

Staff explained that the residents had found driving and shooting particularly challenging, but enjoyed exploring the environment by boat.

The experience proved popular enough that Lucienne noted she intended to ask her children for GTA 6 for Christmas, while Jacqueline suggested installing a console in the communal lounge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A strange deal over on Samsung.com is offering the Galaxy Z Fold 8 for $1,499, a new low price for the hit foldable, but it’s not showing up for all people.

Samsung’s fresh Galaxy Z Fold 8 is usually sold for $1,899 which, in itself, isn’t a bad price for the device. But it’s been available with some kind of discount at basically all times since it released. And, this week, we’re seeing a new low price that brings the foldable down to $1,499.

The discount is available on Samsung.com and cuts $400 off of the price of a fresh Galaxy Z Fold 8 in any configuration. That brings the 256GB model down to $1,499.99, as pictured below.

There are two “catches” with this one.

Firstly, this is a discount if you buy the Fold 8 without a trade-in. Moving to a trade charges the fully $1,899 and applies your credit to that.

According to recent reports, the other is that, strangely, this $400 discount isn’t showing for everyone. As noted when we covered the previous all-time-low earlier this week, $1,549, Samsung.com only indicates a $350 discount to some owners, and there’s no rhyme or reason to it. As for why this is the case, we’re not sure, but it’s unfortunately not uncommon for Samsung.com sales to act a bit inconsistently like this.

In a recent development, whatever the case, if you’re hunting for a Galaxy Z Fold 8, now is very much the time. Whether you’re paying $1,549 or $1,499, it’s still a killer discount. Notably, the Amazon deal still lets you stack a trade-in on top for up to $980 off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newegg is back at it again with a fresh set of combo deals just in time for Black Friday. This 4-item combo offers a massive $369 discount; if you apply it to the RAM, it comes down to $111 and brings back memories of days past. For only $1,549, you get an awesome gaming (and productivity) chip in the Ryzen 9 9950X3D, 32GB of V-Color DDR5-6000 CL30 RAM, a premium Asus ROG Strix X870E-E Gaming Wifi motherboard, and a 2TB Samsung 990 Pro M.2 SSD. Newegg even sweetens the pot with a free 240mm MSI AIO ($85 value). You’re only a couple of parts away from a complete AM5 system with this awesome Newegg deal.

In a recent development, the RAM included in the combo is V-Color Manta XSky. This memory kit has been a commonplace in Newegg bundles for a while now. And though some may not recognize the name, they are quality kits. The sticks sport black heat spreaders and a frosted RGB element across the top and match well with the Asus board. Specs-wise, it’s a 32GB (2x16GB) DDR5-6000 kit with tight timings (CL30-38-38-96 @ 1.35V). Under the hood are SK Hynix ICs, so you do have some headroom if you want to overclock past their rated speed or to tighten them down. AMD’s sweet spot (Price/performance) for AM5 processors is around 6000-6400 MT/s, so these fall into that bucket and pair perfectly with the 9950X3D.

Sources indicate that save big with this 4-item Newegg combo. You get one of the most powerful X3D chips in the Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor (great for gaming and productivity), 32GB of V-Color Manta XSky DDR5-6000 with a low CL30 rating, a solid Asus ROG Strix X870E-E Gaming Wifi motherboard, and a fast 2TB Samsung 990 Pro PCIe 4 x4 drive with speeds to 7,450/6,900 MB/s (R/W). With this combo, you're either getting the RAM for only $110 or the Samsung storage for only $30. Either way, it's a beefy discount for quality components.

According to recent reports, next is the Ryzen 9 9950X3D processor. Before the X3D2 was released in April of this year, this was the flagship X3D SKU and offered not only a lot of cores and threads (16c/32t) but also X3D cache (128MB) on one of the CCDs, which is great for gaming. Clock speeds start at 4.3 GHz, with turbo boosting a couple of cores up to 5.7 GHz. With its clock speeds, core count, and extra cache, this processor is not only great for gaming but also awesome for any PC work that needs more cores and threads, like video editing, 3D rendering, and even running VMs.

Industry observers note that the third part of the combo is the Samsung 990 Pro M.2. This PCIe 4.0 x4 SSD delivers up to 7,250/6,450 MB/s sequential read/write speeds and up to 850K/1,200K IOPS for random reads/writes. This is a very speedy PCIe 4 drive, only eclipsed by more costly PCIe 5-based drives. We reviewed this drive when it was released and loved its strong all-around performance, excellent software (Samsung Magician), and consistent, efficient, cool-running performance.

Last but certainly not least, we reviewed the Asus ROG Strix X870E-E Gaming Wifi motherboard and gave it four stars as one of our best options around the ~$500 price point. This premium offering gives users everything they want out of a motherboard. It has strong power delivery to support the 9950X3D processor, five M.2 sockets (three PCIe 5.0) and four SATA ports for storage, fast networking with 5GbE and 320MHz Wi-Fi, ample USB ports on the rear I/O including dual USB4 (40 Gbps) Type-C ports, and a premium audio solution using the Real ALC4080 codec along with an integrated amplifier. On top of that, it’s packed with “AI” features (Overclocking, Cooling, Cache Boost) and sports a DIY-friendly design.

Sources indicate that if you were waiting for Black Friday week to take the pain out of buying PC components, that time is now. Even if you weren't, that time is still probably now. This 4-item combo with its huge $369 discount is only $1549 and one of the best bundles Newegg has going for those looking for a high-end entry into the AM5 platform and who need good storage too. The combo only lasts until supplies run out, so jump on this stellar deal while you can.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Players have found that music in The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+’s fresh GTA 6-themed secret run was made with Suno, as the free DLC sits at Overwhelmingly Negative recent reviews on Steam.

The run arrived in the same update that brought Repentance+ to PS5, Xbox, and Switch 2 on November 19, a release date publisher Nicalis picked to go head-to-head with GTA 6.

Entering the seed V1CE BSMT unlocks a Vice City-inspired daily run with its own soundtrack, made up of seven songs plus a handful of intros and outros.

A player on the Binding of Isaac subreddit extracted the run’s music from the game files and found several tracks still carrying metadata reading “made with suno,” along with links to the songs on Suno’s site.

The metadata on one track highlights it was created on October 30, 2026, less than three weeks before the patch went live. Other players have since checked the files and confirmed the find.

The run itself is credited to a modder known as Mr. Headcrab, who the original poster notes is “staunchly anti-AI” and had no idea the music was generated.

Valve requires developers to disclose AI-generated content on a game’s Steam page, but Repentance+’s store listing makes no mention of it.

The DLC presently sits at Overwhelmingly Negative recent reviews, with only 10% of 908 reviews from the past 30 days positive, though the same upgrade has also been blamed for breaking mods and causing crashes.

Recent findings suggest that for some fans, the AI music is the final straw. “They used AI when synthwave is like… the easiest genre to make,” one player wrote, in a comment with dozens of upvotes.

The community-run Isaac wiki has since added a note flagging the AI-generated tracks. Nicalis has yet to comment on the music or add a disclosure to the Steam page.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

Recent findings suggest that • A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

Industry observers note that • Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

It has been revealed that • Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

• Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it indicates it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

It has been revealed that limitations and gaps: the page demonstrates different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your plan. It notes to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

Recent findings suggest that GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Industry observers note that strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

According to recent reports, limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and indicates other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and plan prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

According to recent reports, copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it states it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

Limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid plan prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

Sources indicate that originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Industry observers note that strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Industry observers note that limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Sources indicate that limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

Sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

Strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page indicates false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

Sources indicate that the table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

• False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

• Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

In a recent development, • Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

In a recent development, • Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

In a recent development, • Moving targets. Upcoming models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

According to recent reports, • Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

Industry observers note that openAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

It has been revealed that most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

• Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

Recent findings suggest that • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and enhancement as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

• Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

Because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

According to recent reports, group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

Industry observers note that • Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

• Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

It has been revealed that • Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

• Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

Recent findings suggest that they can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

In a recent development, yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sources indicate that sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

In a recent development, AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.
